title: Longitudinal survey: productivity holds steady while developer experience degrades underneath it
summary: Annie Vella and Kelly Blincoe of the University of Auckland ran two survey waves six months apart and matched 95 respondents across both, which is rare in this literature — almost all evidence on AI and developer experience is a single snapshot. Self-reported productivity was flat and high: 84% reported improvement at both points. Experience moved the other way. The share of matched participants reporting a worsened experience on at least one dimension nearly doubled, from 14% to 27%. Flow state and cognitive load both declined, while feedback loops improved — meaning the gains and losses landed on different dimensions rather than cancelling out. 82% reported spending less time writing code, which the authors characterise as a shift toward 'supervisory engineering work'. The finding that matters for leaders is the decoupling itself: the authors' 'productivity-experience paradox' means the metric most organisations watch would show nothing while the thing that predicts attrition moved.
dataCollectedPeriod: October 2024 to April 2025 (two waves, six months apart)
whyItMatters: Productivity and experience moved independently over six months in the same people. Any dashboard tracking only output would have reported a healthy period, which is a direct argument for measuring experience separately rather than inferring it.
The deterioration accelerated between waves rather than appearing at adoption. Organisations that surveyed once at rollout and saw nothing alarming should assume that reading has expired.
Feedback loops improved while flow and cognitive load worsened. Composite developer-experience scores will net these against each other and show stability that is not there.
recommendedActions: Run developer-experience measurement on a repeated matched-cohort basis rather than as one-off snapshots, and report flow, cognitive load and feedback loops separately instead of as a single index.
Stop treating stable productivity as evidence that an AI rollout is going well; pair it with an experience measure before drawing that conclusion.
risksAndCaveats: Fieldwork ran October 2024 to April 2025 and predates the agentic tooling most teams now use. It is evidence that the decoupling can happen, not a current reading of its size; the mechanism has almost certainly intensified since.

Voluntary online survey with 60% retention between waves. Attrition between waves is plausibly non-random — participants whose experience worsened most may be over- or under-represented among those who returned, and the direction is unknowable.
All measures are self-reported perceptions, including the productivity measure. The paradox is between two self-reports, not between an objective metric and a felt one.

Lead author Annie Vella also writes publicly on this theme; her essay on the software engineering identity crisis is already on this radar (2026-02-19-01). This item is the separate empirical study, not a restatement of that piece.
